extracted.intended_audience: readers of entertainment/TV news, followers of comedy/Hasan Minhaj, and people interested in ethics of stand-up and political satire
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for how comedians (especially political/stand-up comics) may use embellishment, how audiences and media should evaluate factual vs 'emotional' truth, and what responsibilities performers have when their material involves real people or serious events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional truth versus factual truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “The emotional truth is first. The factual truth is secondary.” (quote from Minhaj as discussed in the article).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by the comedian to justify embellishment in stand-up to convey feeling and impact. Article notes Minhaj says this line referred to his persona as a storyteller, not his role as a political comedian/host. The guidance implies emotional truth can be prioritized in stand-up storytelling but must be qualified when the performer has political/journalistic responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of embellishment/hyperbole as a tool of stand-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Minhaj admits he 'selectively presents information and embellishes to make a point' and defends 'hyperbole' and other 'tools of stand-up'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embellishment can be a legitimate storytelling device to create shock, humor, or emotional resonance (e.g., creating a hospital scene to put the audience in shock). However, performers should apologize and correct when embellishments meaningfully distort serious facts or harm others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher factual standards for political comedy and journalistic formats
rubrics_metrics.description: For series like 'The Daily Show' and 'Patriot Act', 'the truth comes first' and 'fact checking was paramount'; 'Fact-checking at 'Patriot Act' was extremely rigorous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comedy intersects with political reporting or infotainment, rigorous fact-checking and adherence to factual accuracy are expected. Material presented in journalistic or quasi-journalistic contexts should meet higher verification standards than purely personal stand-up anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish persona/storyteller from real-life claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Minhaj says the 'emotional truth' comment referred to his persona as a storyteller and not to his role as a political comedian or host.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedians should clearly distinguish between a stage persona and factual claims about real events/people; failure to make that distinction can lead audiences and reporters to treat comedic stories as factual reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide corroborating evidence when disputing or making serious claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Minhaj presented emails and other evidence to counter the New Yorker account (e.g., leaked emails from 'Bethany'); the New Yorker cited interviews with more than 20 people and fact-checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stories allege real events or contestations, cite documents, witness testimony, or other verifiable evidence. Both performers and reporters should base public claims on corroboration to resolve conflicting narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise about factual details; small changes can alter perception
rubrics_metrics.description: A detail change—rejection occurring on a doorstep versus days before—shaped how the prom story was portrayed and perceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate timing and setting details matter because they can change the implication or motive of a story. Avoid altering specifics that materially change how events are interpreted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inventing or misattributing real individuals; disclose composites
rubrics_metrics.description: Minhaj acknowledged that the character 'Brother Eric' was an amalgamation of undercover agents and not the specific real individual (Craig Monteilh) implied by the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If composite characters or fictionalized amalgams are used, disclose that to avoid implying a real person's identity. Misattributing actions to a named or identifiable real person is unethical and can cause reputational harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not fabricate details that create or exaggerate harm to others
rubrics_metrics.description: Minhaj admitted embellishing an 'anthrax scare' scene—creating a hospital scene implying his daughter was hospitalized when she was not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabrications that suggest injury, threats, or medical harm to real people (especially children) are particularly serious; performers should refrain from inventing or dramatizing such events in ways that mislead audiences or stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage transparently and timely with subjects and critics
rubrics_metrics.description: Minhaj provided evidence, reached out to the woman involved (invited her to events, connected her with fact-checkers), and later published a response video addressing the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When controversies arise, proactively engaging with affected individuals, publishing clarifications or rebuttals, and making evidence available can help resolve disputes. Timely public responses and apologies when appropriate are part of responsible practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media/reporting standards: corroboration and multiple sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The New Yorker defended its piece as 'carefully reported and fact-checked' based on interviews with more than 20 people including staffers, security team members, and people who were the subject of his stand-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic coverage of a comedian's claims should rely on multiple independent sources, documentation, and rigorous fact-checking before asserting fabrications or wrongdoing.
